stem: An opioid-naive 82-year-old with a hip fracture is prescribed morphine for severe acute pain. Which dosing and monitoring principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Use cautious dose selection near the low end of the appropriate range, titrate slowly to response, and frequently reassess for sedation and respiratory depression.
options.B: Use the usual younger-adult starting approach based mainly on pain severity, then reduce the dose if central nervous system or respiratory effects become evident.
options.C: Avoid morphine because advanced age makes opioid therapy inappropriate for severe fracture pain even when alternative analgesics are inadequate.
options.D: Choose the initial dose without considering age-related renal or cardiac changes, then rely on routine pain scores to determine whether subsequent doses are safe.

rationale: Current DailyMed labeling states that adults age 65 years or older may have increased sensitivity to morphine and that dose selection should be cautious, usually starting at the low end of the dosing range because hepatic, renal, cardiac, comorbidity, and concomitant-drug factors are more common. Respiratory depression is the chief opioid risk in older adults, particularly after large initial doses in opioid-naive patients. The label directs slow titration with frequent reevaluation for central nervous system and respiratory depression. Therefore A is correct. B waits for toxicity after a more aggressive initial approach. C incorrectly treats older age as a reason to withhold an otherwise indicated opioid. D ignores geriatric physiologic factors and inadequate monitoring domains.
educational_objective: For an opioid-naive older adult receiving morphine, select the initial dose cautiously near the low end of the appropriate range, titrate slowly, and frequently reassess central nervous system and respiratory status.
source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. National Library of Medicine
source_locator: Use in Specific Populations 8.5 Geriatric Use: adults age 65 or older may have increased sensitivity to morphine; use caution in dose selection, usually starting at the low end of the dosing range; respiratory depression is the chief risk in elderly opioid-treated patients and has occurred after large initial doses in opioid-naive patients; titrate slowly and frequently reevaluate for CNS and respiratory depression. Dosage and Administration 2.1 and 2.4: use the lowest effective dosage, individualize dosing, and continually reevaluate response and adverse reactions.
source_claim_supported: Older adults may have increased morphine sensitivity; geriatric dosing should be cautious, usually begin near the low end, be titrated slowly, and include frequent CNS and respiratory-depression reassessment.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed pp. 38–41: titrate medication dosage based on assessment and ordered parameters; evaluate client response to medication; administer medications for pain management; recognize adverse medication effects.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — geriatric morphine dosing, titration, and respiratory monitoring
correction_summary: Rebuilt all choices to remove absolute-word cueing and use realistic geriatric opioid-management errors involving aggressive initial dosing, inappropriate age-based avoidance, and failure to incorporate age-related physiology into monitoring.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Opioid analgesia — morphine dosing and monitoring in an opioid-naive older adult
audit_findings.stem: PASS — provides older age, opioid-naive status, and severe acute pain, all directly relevant to initial morphine safety.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly matches current geriatric labeling for cautious low-end selection, slow titration, and frequent CNS/respiratory reassessment; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — pain severity matters, but the label specifically cautions against aggressive initial dosing in older opioid-naive patients and requires proactive monitoring.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — age increases risk but does not make morphine categorically inappropriate when opioid analgesia is indicated.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — geriatric hepatic, renal, cardiac and concomitant-disease factors are specifically relevant to dose selection; pain scores alone are insufficient safety monitoring.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that fully incorporates both geriatric dose-selection and monitoring guidance.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B delays adjustment until toxicity, C inappropriately withholds therapy based on age, and D ignores geriatric physiologic risk factors.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all options are comparable in length and clinical specificity, with no keyed-only absolute wording.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies directly includes titration, pain medication, response evaluation and adverse-effect monitoring.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether severe pain should justify standard adult initiation or whether age alone should favor avoidance; current labeling specifically calls for cautious low-end starting selection and slow titration rather than either extreme, leaving A uniquely correct.
